column8: Fri 20 Nov: 2.0 or 3d: the conceit's rule given its founding pedigree; Hamilton's maxim (1790 report, read at source) joins each debt to its means, and with row 4 the turn is that a state can promise first because it can tax while a writer cannot; never to the letter in quotation marks as his; read cold before it takes a slot.

Fri 20 Nov: the spine as a market price: the Confederation's promises, with no power to tax, sold at 15 to 25 cents in April 1789; one clause beside row 1 at most; a traded war debt, never a price put on Laura's figure.

Fri 20 Nov: store, beside row 2: never the same promise across 1789-1791 (old certificates became new stock worth about $75 per $100, row 11); the 6% stock was at 70 four months after the Act and part of its rise to par was the Bank scrip boom, so say it rose as the revenue arrived, never belief followed money.

Fri 20 Nov: 2.0 or 3d with row 1: the 1790 Act pledged money to be provided hereafter, pencil in the conceit's terms, which a state can do because it can tax; fix the IPS l.9 clause to income that can come later and smaller in the same downturn, never falls in the same recession as co-sponsors' budgets (card Q50: can, never together).

Fri 20 Nov: 3d, the team's sentence before her words, never in them: Hamilton's price of a promise is its size times the chance it continues; fix: the top rests on shares of the late-2032 iBond fund, bought twice, which pay net asset value on a board-set end, so the chance behind it is the Treasury's plus the fund's, never owned Treasuries alone (blind judges' finding 1).

Fri 20 Nov: store: opinion is the soul of credit is read at source, but Hamilton argued against delay and Laura delays stating to the move on purpose, so it cannot explain 3d's one figure without the reader seeing the break; never as a point about appearances.

Fri 20 Nov: 2.0 or 3d: the same act honest or not by its place in the sequence, in Hamilton's own words, is the spine's buy first and state second; fix: the top, never $115,000, is a forecast before the move and owned after it, since the figure stated is whatever the move buys and $115,000 is today's central figure resting on shares earning above about 3.4% a year (NUMBERS 8v).

Fri 20 Nov: wording guard for any part that names Hamilton: he did not pay the old domestic debt as written (his own words, read at source; $1,696,563.43 budgeted at 4%); never Hamilton paid every creditor in full, never to the letter as his words; binds rows 1-7.
Fri 20 Nov: twin of row 8: the Act's preamble says what Hamilton's words say; the Garber point is unread and contradicts itself (paid as written, yet the French at about 80 cents), so it stays out.
Fri 20 Nov: store: the mechanics behind row 11's haircut ($66.67 of 6% stock and $33.33 deferred per $100; refusers paid only the accepters' rate for 1791); too dense for prose.

Fri 20 Nov: 3c or 3d, one clause at most: American credit began with a restated promise (about $75 per $100 at market on 31 Dec 1790, Hall and Sargent, read at source), a step the plan never needs since nothing is stated before it is owned; say a stated range is never restated, never that it cannot move (NUMBERS 3, an early fund end at zero interest).

Fri 20 Nov: store: Hamilton's voluntary in fact, as well as in name is read at source; the link to the 0.5% cut and the rounding is loose, since co-sponsors are not creditors whose terms are restated.

Fri 20 Nov: 3c contrast candidate: Hamilton priced America's founding swap on a forecast (probabilities are always a rational ground of contract, read at source) between parties who could refuse; Laura's stated figures carry no forecast and the 7.5% stays in Table 2's note; competes with Neyman for 3c, so read cold first.

Fri 20 Nov: store, or half a clause in 2.0 with row 26: 1790's debt had no date (an annuity redeemable at the government's pleasure), so on its date is the part later Treasuries added; trivia unless row 15 uses it.

Fri 20 Nov: Table 3 row 4's reason in one clause: the right to repay early moved from the government in 1790 to no one for Treasuries since 1985 and to each fund's board for the five fund rungs (CANON C2: end early, merge or extend); an early end pays the fund's value early, never cancels, and at zero interest can leave a payment short (NUMBERS 3).

Fri 20 Nov: store: Hamilton's first holder, or his assignee is the root of a Treasury paying whoever holds it; the step to UCC 8-503 is loose (hers is a book entry held for her, not a claim to a specific identifiable thing, Q157-032), so never as the legal basis of owned.

Fri 20 Nov: store: the House's 36 to 13 rejection of Madison's discrimination (read at source) is row 26's owner test; its use line (a Treasury needs no one's view of Laura) serves no part on its own.

Fri 20 Nov: 2.0, half a clause beside the definition of ink: the debt sits in the Constitution twice, Article VI for the Confederation's debts and the 14th Amendment s.4 for all public debt authorized by law; a strong true word with no default caveat attached (Book 19).

Fri 20 Nov: store, or 3e's single statement of the default premise: the Union's debt shall not be questioned and the Confederacy's is void, in one section; said once at most, since dwelling on default is what Books 3, 5 and 19 forbid; a US default is the paper is CONCEIT's store, not 3e's one turn (erase every pencil line).

Fri 20 Nov: twin of H5-041 (Perry's holding), with the exact words read at source for when H5-041 is quoted; its use line breaks H4-030's guard: the 1933 rewrite stood, so never that a Treasury's terms cannot be rewritten.

Fri 20 Nov: store: the gold-clause withdrawal of consent is true, but 5118(c)(2), read at source today, keeps claims up to the face or nominal dollar value, so the use line is false for a dollar figure: never no court can make the US pay or the US pays only because it chooses; if used, the statute that barred gold claims kept the dollar figure suable.

Fri 20 Nov: store: Hamilton's moral agent (1795, quoted in Perry) is read at source, but the use line is false: owning does not take away Laura's power to vary, since she can still sell (AHA_REGISTER, nobody can run on the plan); what owning removes is the figure's dependence on markets.

Fri 20 Nov: store, or half a clause after row 26's 1933 test: over 80% of gold-clause holders rolled into new Treasury issues (CRS R44704, re-read today word for word); holders lost against what they had expected, so never no loss.

Fri 20 Nov: wording guard for 2.0 and 3e: the US missed interest due in Boston on 1 Oct 1814 (CRS's sentence re-read today word for word), so the record runs since the War of 1812; never never defaulted or two centuries; a true span, never a caveat on Treasuries (Book 19).

Fri 20 Nov: 2.0's evidence for row 26: fix late once by days, since some 1979 checks were up to about three weeks late (Q138-001, Q15-015) while book-entry holders were unaffected (CRS, re-read today), the form Laura's are held in; paid every dollar figure since the War of 1812 is Keel's reading of three episodes, never CRS's words.

Fri 20 Nov: 2.0, one clause after the definition, the card's strongest idea: but on its date did not hold in 1979, when paper checks were paid days to weeks late; fix: the owner and the dollar figure held, and the date slipped once, on paper checks, while book entries like hers were paid on time (CRS; Q15-015); 1790's owners were paid in restated stock (row 11); read cold before it takes a slot.

Fri 20 Nov: 3a, where the Treasury's record stops and the plan's margin starts, as the blind judges asked: five payments rest on fund shares paying net asset value; fix: the 0.5% covers fund costs beyond the fee, not an end moved by a board, since with cash waiting at zero an early end can leave a payment short (up to $14,688 for a fund ended February 2027; none at today's market rates, NUMBERS 3), which Table 3 row 4 watches.

Fri 20 Nov: store: Lynch (1934) held war-risk insurance contracts against the Economy Act; the tie to IPS l.17's market fall is loose; quote only the words read, since the sentence's end was not read at source.
Fri 20 Nov: store only: the 1790 assumption bought allies for federal taxes; serves no part.

Fri 20 Nov: 3d or 3b, one clause, never in her words: a rescue once given is read as a promise (Sargent's lecture read at source), so half the shares stay promised to no one and 3d names one figure; anything she gives later is her separate choice (CANON D12); leave out the 70%, read only in a search extract of Henning and Kessler.
Fri 20 Nov: the second half of row 30's story (the refusal cost US credit in Europe in 1842); one clause with row 30 if any, never on its own.
Fri 20 Nov: store: Congress's 1840s test (a glorious national purpose against local projects) maps loosely; never read as a standing offer of her flexibility.
